subject: chemistry
question_text: What is a spontaneous process? Give an example.

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This question comes from the enumeration sweep of the Thermodynamics syllabus: the book uses the word spontaneous in its second-law and Gibbs-energy answers (VSAQ 6, VSAQ 8) but never asks what a spontaneous process is. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry, so the two-book union check is PENDING — a second source may show this asked. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: A spontaneous process is one that takes
place on its own, without continuous
It has a definite natural direction and
does not reverse on its own.
steps.why: The one-way character is the point: the reverse change is possible, but only when work is supplied from outside.
common_mistakes: Writing that spontaneous means fast — rusting is spontaneous and slow; speed is a separate question.
steps.memory_tip: Spontaneous says which way, never how fast.
steps.margin_note: On its own and one direction are the two ideas.

steps.label: Examples and criterion
lines: Examples: heat flows from a hot body to a
cold body; a gas expands into an empty
vessel; iron rusts in moist air.
At constant T and p the test is ΔG < 0.

lines.text: Spontaneous: proceeds on its own; ΔG is negative

steps.why: Each example runs in one direction only, and none of them needs outside work to proceed — that is what the definition describes.
common_mistakes: Giving a driven process as the example — charging a battery or pumping water uphill needs outside work, so neither is spontaneous.
steps.memory_tip: Three stock examples: hot to cold, gas into vacuum, iron to rust.
steps.margin_note: One example earns the mark; the ΔG line connects it to Gibbs energy.
